It is plainly not on the ground: its bottom edge sits roughly a hundred pixels above where the grass line runs between the front wheel's contact patch and the rear wheel's contact patch, so it is hanging on the bodywork rather than standing on the turf.

## How you can tell it was never a running wheel

**1. The spare is filthy while all four running wheels are clean.** Brightening the shadows shows that the near-side front tyre, the off-side front tyre and the rear tyre all have clean black rubber, clean black wire spokes and bright, polished knock-off spinners. The only things stuck to them are dry grass strands and a little road dust — no mud at all. The spare, by contrast, is plastered in dried grey-tan mud, thickest of anything on the car. If the spare had done the muddy driving and had then been swapped off, the wheel that replaced it would have been fitted and driven in that same mud and would look dirty too. Not one of the four is.

**2. The mud on the spare is unevenly distributed around the circle, which a rotating wheel cannot manage.** On the spare, the lower and rearward portion of the tyre, the lower rim and the area around the hub are heavily caked, while the top of the tyre — roughly from ten o'clock round through twelve to two o'clock — is clean black rubber with crisp, empty tread grooves. A wheel that actually rolls through mud keeps turning, so every part of its circumference passes through the same mud and it comes out dirty **uniformly all the way round**. A clean top and a dirty bottom can only survive on a wheel that stayed put. The dirt on the spare is also arranged as a fan or starburst radiating outwards from around the hub — the signature of a spray arriving from one direction and striking a fixed surface.

**3. The mud sits on the surface as separate splash spots rather than being packed into the tread.** At high magnification, the dirt on the spare's tread is a scatter of individual flecks and blobs lying on top of the rubber, with the tread blocks and grooves still visible and largely empty underneath. A tyre that has been driven through mud gets mud pressed and packed down into the grooves and smeared across the crown by contact with the ground. None of that is present here.

**4. The spare's dirt matches the stationary bodywork, not the rotating parts.** The outer face of the rear wing and the inner face of the front wing are covered in exactly the same dried grey speckling as the spare. All three sit in the same firing line — directly behind the front wheel, which flings mud rearwards and outwards as it turns. The spare was simply one more fixed surface standing in that spray, and because it is mounted broadside to it, it caught the most.

**5. The pattern is internally consistent.** The bodywork is still muddy, so the car has not been washed since the drive; the road wheels are clean anyway, because a spinning tyre throws its mud off centrifugally and scrubs its tread clean again on firm ground. That is precisely the state the photograph shows: clean rotating parts, dirty stationary parts — and the spare belongs firmly in the second group.

## The obvious counter-argument, and why it fails

One might argue that because the spare is the dirtiest wheel on the car, it must have been the one doing the work. But that gets it backwards. Being dirtiest is the mark of a surface that could not shed what hit it. A running wheel self-cleans; a wheel bolted to the side of the body does not. And the three decisive details above — the clean upper tread, the unpacked tread grooves, and the identical spatter on the wings and body panels alongside it — all point the same way.

# Answer

**Yes.** The wheel now hanging on the side of the car as the spare was being used as one of the four running wheels when the car was driven through mud. After that muddy drive the muddy wheel was taken off, a clean wheel was fitted in its place, and the muddy wheel was put back on the spare carrier beside the door.

## How you can tell

You can tell from the mud: which wheel carries it, where on that wheel it sits, and which wheels carry none.

1. **The spare is the only muddy wheel.** Zooming in on the spare wheel strapped to the side of the body (just behind the front fender, beside the door) shows dried, light-brown mud caked around the hub where the wire spokes meet it, spreading outward along the spokes, and speckled around the rim. Dried mud is also packed into the grooves of the spare's tread and smeared over the tread blocks and sidewall, most heavily around the lower part of the tire as it now hangs. Mud gets packed into tread grooves and thrown across a hub and spokes like this only when a wheel is rotating on the ground through mud. A wheel that simply hangs on the side of the car never touches the ground and never spins, so it cannot pick up mud that way.

2. **The running wheels are clean.** The near-side front wheel and near-side rear wheel that the car is standing on have glossy, clean black spokes, clean rims and sidewalls, and bright polished chrome knock-off hub nuts. Their tread grooves hold nothing but a few green grass clippings picked up driving onto the show field. The far-side front wheel, visible under the radiator beside the headlamp, also has clean black spokes. If these wheels had been on the car during the muddy drive, they would be at least as muddy as the spare. They are not.

3. **The mud on the spare did not come from the front wheel spraying it while it hung on the side.** One might wonder whether the spare got dirty in its side mount from mud flung back by the front tire just ahead of it. The pattern argues against that. Spray from the front wheel would land on the forward-facing edge of the spare's tread and sidewall, the part nearest the front wheel. Instead the heaviest mud is on the outward-facing spoke side of the wheel, concentrated at the hub and over the rearward half of the spokes and rim, with the forward-facing spokes comparatively clean. That is how mud lands on a wheel that is itself rolling and spinning through mud, with the mud thrown onto the hub and carried outward along the spokes.

4. **The bodywork still records the muddy drive, but the wheels under it do not.** The rear fender is peppered with dried mud speckles thrown up by a tire, and the front fender carries a lighter dusting, so the car really was driven through mud with its wheels flinging it at the wings. Yet the wheel sitting directly under that mud-speckled rear fender is spotless, with clean rubber and grass against it at the ground. If the owner had simply washed the car afterwards, the flat, easy-to-reach fenders would have been cleaned before the fiddly wire spokes and tread grooves, not the other way round. Dirty fenders with clean wheels means the wheels were changed, not washed.

## Conclusion

The only wheel showing the evidence of rolling through mud is the one now carried on the side as the spare, and the wheels now on the ground show none of it, while the fenders show the car did go through mud. Therefore the spare must have been fitted as a running wheel during the muddy drive (for example to replace a punctured wheel), and was swapped back to the spare mount afterwards when the clean wheel was refitted. Which corner it was on cannot be read from the photo with certainty, though the rear fender on the visible side is the muddiest.

## Detailed Evidence

Three distinct visual proofs demonstrate that the spare tire was stationary and mounted on the side of the car when the mud was encountered:

### 1. Highly Localized Mud Pattern (No Centrifugal Rotation)
* **The Physics of Rotation:** If this tire had been mounted on the ground and running while the car drove through mud, it would have rotated thousands of times. The centrifugal force and continuous contact with the ground would distribute the mud, dirt, and water relatively evenly across the entire 360-degree circumference of the tire sidewall, wheel rim, and spokes.
* **The Observed Pattern:** On the spare tire, the dried mud is heavily concentrated in a single localized area: the **lower-right (rear-facing) quadrant** of the tire sidewall, rim, and wire spokes. This uneven, static splatter pattern is only possible if the wheel was stationary when the mud hit it.

### 2. Clean, Uncompacted Tread Grooves
* **The Physics of Tread Contact:** A tire rolling through mud compresses the soil, packing mud deep into the tread grooves across its entire circumference.
* **The Observed Pattern:** The deep tread grooves of the spare tire (clearly visible on its left-hand side) are completely clean, empty, and pristine. There is no compacted mud or soil residue inside any of the grooves. The mud present on the bottom-right of the tire is merely a superficial splatter on the outer surface of the rubber, not compacted into the tread.

### 3. Directional Spray from the Rear Drive Wheel
* **Source of the Mud:** This vintage Bentley is a rear-wheel-drive car. When driving through mud or if the vehicle becomes stuck, the rear drive wheels spin rapidly and fling mud both backwards and forwards/upwards.
* **The Splatter Alignment:** The mud on the spare tire is located on its lower-rear side (the bottom-right quadrant in the image), facing the rear wheels. This matches the exact trajectory of mud being thrown forward and upward from the spinning rear tire. The mud splattered across the stationary spare's outer face (rim and spokes) and the adjacent rear fender, confirming the spare was simply in the "line of fire" of the rear wheel's spray while mounted on the side of the car.
